24–25. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are these four? They are: the self-nature of false discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the self-nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the self-nature of perfect accomplishment (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the self-nature of the ultimate reality (*dharmatā-svabhāva*). Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of false discrimination? It is the attachment to names and signs (*nāmanimitta*) as being real entities, based on the false discrimination of objects that do not exist. This is called the self-nature of false discrimination. What is the self-nature of dependent origination? It is the manifestation of all phenomena arising from the habit-energy of false discrimination, appearing like a dream or a magical illusion. This is called the self-nature of dependent origination. What is the self-nature of perfect accomplishment? It is the realization that the self-nature of dependent origination is devoid of the characteristics of false discrimination; it is the non-dual realm of suchness, which is the object of noble wisdom. This is called the self-nature of perfect accomplishment. What is the self-nature of the ultimate reality? It is the state in which the self-natures of both false discrimination and dependent origination are completely transcended, and one abides in the Tathāgata-garbha, which is the realm of the Dharma-body. This is called the self-nature of the ultimate reality. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should train yourself to thoroughly understand these four kinds of self-nature. By doing so, you and other Bodhisattvas will quickly attain the stage of Buddhahood. Thus it is said: The self-nature of false discrimination, The self-nature of dependent origination, The self-nature of perfect accomplishment, And the self-nature of the ultimate reality— These four kinds of self-nature Are taught by the Buddhas. If one understands them well, One shall quickly become a Buddha.

28.34. If one were to ask, "What is the cause for the non-arising of the afflictions? the answer is: it is the absence of the conditions for their arising. Furthermore, what are the conditions for the arising of the afflictions? They are the presence of the objects of perception, the lack of mindfulness, and the improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*). What is improper mental attention? It is the conceptualization that apprehends signs (*nimittodgrahaṇavikalpa*) regarding those very same objects of perception. What is the conceptualization that apprehends signs? It is the conceptualization that apprehends characteristics (*lakṣaṇodgrahaṇavikalpa*) regarding those very same objects of perception. What is the conceptualization that apprehends characteristics? It is the conceptualization that apprehends the nature of things (*svabhāvavikalpa*) regarding those very same objects of perception. What is the conceptualization that apprehends the nature of things? It is the conceptualization that apprehends distinctions (*viśeṣavikalpa*) regarding those very same objects of perception. What is the conceptualization that apprehends distinctions? It is the conceptualization that apprehends attachment (*abhiniveśavikalpa*) regarding those very same objects of perception. What is the conceptualization that apprehends attachment? It is the conceptualization that apprehends the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭivikalpa*) regarding those very same objects of perception. What is the conceptualization that apprehends the view of self? It is the conceptualization that apprehends the view of mine (*mamakāradṛṣṭivikalpa*) regarding those very same objects of perception. The Characteristics of the Accomplished Yogin (yuktasya lakṣaṇam) When the yogin has attained mastery over the mind, he remains established in his own nature even while engaged in worldly activities. He does not perceive the objects of the senses as distinct from himself, nor does he perceive himself as separate from those objects. He beholds all things as identical with his own self, and his self as identical with all things. He sees no difference between the subject and the object, and thus he is liberated from the duality of "I" and "mine. Even when walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he remains ever absorbed in the state of samādhi. His speech and actions are spontaneous and effortless, arising from his deep realization rather than from deliberate effort. He is free from attachment, aversion, and delusion; he is neither elated by gain nor dejected by loss. He regards praise and blame, pleasure and pain, honor and dishonor with equal indifference. To him, a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are all the same. He is not moved by the fluctuations of fortune or the opinions of others. His mind is steady, tranquil, and unwavering, like a lamp in a windless place. Though surrounded by the world, he remains detached, like a lotus leaf untouched by water. He does not seek liberation as something external to be attained, for he realizes that liberation is his very own nature. Thus, the yogin who has become one with the Absolute is said to be truly accomplished.

The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, it is not only now that I have performed this great miracle; in the past, too, I performed this great miracle, which was unprecedented among gods and humans. The venerable Ānanda asked: “At what time, Blessed One, did the Blessed One perform this great miracle? The Blessed One said: “In the past, Ānanda, there was a king named Mahāsudarśana, who was a universal monarch, a righteous ruler of the world, possessing the seven treasures and the four kinds of miraculous power. He traveled through the four continents, bringing peace and security to all beings. At that time, Ānanda, King Mahāsudarśana went to the Himalayas and saw a mountain peak made of the seven precious substances, adorned with various jewels. Seeing it, he thought: ‘This mountain peak is beautiful; it would be excellent if I were to build a palace here. Having thought this, he commanded his ministers: ‘Go, my ministers, and build for me a palace on this mountain peak. “Then, Ānanda, the ministers, having received the king’s command, built a palace on that mountain peak.

It was a hundred yojanas in length and breadth, and its height reached fifty yojanas. It was adorned with the seven precious substances and filled with various celestial delights. When the palace was completed, they informed the king: ‘Sire, the palace is finished. “Then, Ānanda, King Mahāsudarśana ascended the palace and sat upon a throne made of the seven precious substances. At that moment, the entire palace trembled and shook. Seeing this, the king thought: ‘What is the cause, what is the reason, for this palace to tremble and shake? Then, Ānanda, the king reflected: ‘I have heard from the sages of old that when a universal monarch sits upon the throne, the palace trembles and shakes. Having understood this, he was filled with joy and satisfaction. “This, Ānanda, is the second great miracle of the Tathāgata, which has never before been seen by gods or humans. Notes 327–346 • Regarding the phrase "the nature of phenomena is not established": this refers to the fact that all phenomena lack inherent existence (*svabhāva*). It is not that phenomena do not exist at all, but rather that they do not exist by way of their own intrinsic nature. This is the core of the Madhyamaka view. • Concerning the distinction between "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*) and "ultimate" (*paramārtha*): the conventional is that which appears to the deluded mind of ordinary beings, while the ultimate is the mode of being as it is, realized through non-conceptual wisdom. • On the subject of "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*): this is the fundamental principle that nothing arises independently; everything arises in dependence upon causes and conditions. The realization of dependent origination is the antidote to the ignorance that grasps at things as being self-existent. • As for the statement "emptiness is not a nihilistic void": emptiness does not mean that things are utterly non-existent. Rather, it means that things are empty of the specific, reified characteristics that the ignorant mind imputes upon them. Emptiness is the very basis for the possibility of change and function. • Regarding the "two truths": the conventional truth consists of the world of names, forms, and causal efficiency as experienced by sentient beings. The ultimate truth is the absence of inherent existence within those very phenomena. These two are not contradictory but are mutually inclusive in the sense that the conventional is the locus of the ultimate. • On the topic of "compassion" (*karuṇā*): this is the altruistic resolve to liberate all beings from suffering. It is considered the root of the Mahāyāna path, for without compassion, the bodhisattva vow cannot arise. • Concerning the "perfections" (*pāramitā*): these are the six (or ten) qualities—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—which must be practiced to the point of perfection in order to attain Buddhahood. • Regarding the "three bodies of a Buddha" (*trikāya*): the *dharmakāya* is the embodiment of ultimate reality; the *sambhogakāya* is the enjoyment body visible to advanced bodhisattvas; and the *nirmāṇakāya* is the emanation body that appears in the world to guide ordinary beings. • On the subject of "the stages of the path" (*lam rim*): this refers to the systematic progression through the levels of realization, beginning with the generation of the awakening mind (*bodhicitta*) and culminating in the attainment of the state of a Buddha. • Regarding the "four immeasurables" (*catvāry apramāṇāni*): these are loving-kindness, compassion, empathetic joy, and equanimity. They serve to purify the mind and prepare it for the cultivation of the perfections. • Concerning the "refutation of the self" (*ātman*): the self is refuted because it is found to be neither identical to nor distinct from the aggregates (*skandha*). Such a self is merely a mental construct and lacks any objective reality. • On the topic of "the nature of the mind": the mind is described as luminous by nature (*prakṛtiprabhāsvara*), yet temporarily obscured by adventitious stains. Through meditation, these stains are cleared away, revealing the mind's innate clarity. • Regarding "the practice of mantra": this involves the recitation of mantras and the visualization of deities (*devatā*) as a method to accelerate the purification of obscurations and the accumulation of merit. • Concerning the "intermediate state" (*antarābhava*): this is the transitional phase between death and rebirth. It is a subtle body that exists until the conditions for a new birth are met. • On the subject of "the three poisons": these are attachment, aversion, and ignorance. They are the primary causes of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and must be transformed through the practice of the Dharma. • Regarding "the nature of samsara": it is characterized by suffering and is driven by the karmic actions and afflictions of sentient beings. Liberation from samsara requires the cessation of these causes. • Concerning "the nature of nirvana": this is the state of permanent liberation from suffering, characterized by peace and the cessation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). • On the topic of "the relationship between cause and effect": this emphasizes the infallibility of karma. Every intentional action produces a corresponding result, whether in this life or in future ones. • Regarding "the nature of the Buddha": a Buddha is one who has fully awakened to the nature of reality and possesses infinite qualities of wisdom and compassion. A Buddha is not a creator god, but a perfected being who serves as a teacher and refuge for all. • Concerning "the nature of the practitioner": a practitioner is one who applies the teachings to their own life, maintaining ethical discipline, cultivating meditation, and dedicating themselves to the welfare of others. • On the subject of "the nature of the teaching": the Dharma is the medicine for the diseases of the mind. It is divided into the Buddha’s words (*buddhavacana*) and the treatises (*śāstra*) composed by realized masters to explain those words.

• Regarding "the nature of the Sangha": the Sangha consists of those who have entered the path and are practicing it correctly. They are the community of practitioners who support one another in the pursuit of liberation. • Concerning "the nature of the world": the world is a product of collective karma and is subject to constant flux. It is not created by a single being, but arises through the interdependence of countless factors. • On the topic of "the nature of time": time is a conceptual construct used to describe the sequence of events. In the ultimate sense, time is empty of inherent existence, just like all other phenomena. • Regarding "the nature of space": space is the absence of obstruction. It is not a physical entity but a condition that allows for movement and the existence of material objects. • Concerning "the nature of dreams": dreams are mental experiences that lack external reality. They illustrate how our perceptions can be deceptive and how the mind projects its own constructs onto experience. • On the subject of "the nature of illusions": illusions are produced by the manipulation of sensory conditions. They appear real to the observer but have no substance. This analogy is used to show that all phenomena are like illusions. • Regarding "the nature of echoes": an echo is a sound produced by the reflection of a voice. It has no independent origin. This illustrates how our thoughts and perceptions often arise in dependence on external stimuli. • Concerning "the nature of mirages": a mirage appears to be water to a person in the desert, but there is no water there. This demonstrates how ignorance leads us to perceive things that do not truly exist. • On the topic of "the nature of reflections": a reflection in a mirror is not the actual object, yet it resembles it. This shows that our mental images of reality are not the reality itself, though they correspond to it in certain ways. • Regarding "the nature of the mind in meditation": during deep states of concentration, the mind becomes clear and stable. This is a temporary state that can lead to the realization of the ultimate nature when properly integrated with wisdom. • Concerning "the nature of the afterlife": the continuity of consciousness ensures that the results of one's actions will follow one beyond this life. This provides the basis for moral responsibility and the pursuit of long-term spiritual goals. • On the subject of "the nature of death": death is the dissolution of the physical body and the transition to a new state of existence. It is a natural process that all beings must face. • Regarding "the nature of rebirth": rebirth occurs due to the force of past karma and the presence of craving. It is the mechanism by which sentient beings continue their journey through cyclic existence. • Concerning "the nature of the Dharma protectors": these are enlightened beings who have pledged to safeguard the teachings and assist practitioners. They are not to be confused with worldly spirits or demons. • On the topic of "the nature of the Three Jewels": the Buddha is the teacher, the Dharma is the path, and the Sangha is the companions on the journey. Together, they constitute the supreme refuge for all beings. • Regarding "the nature of the vows": the vows are commitments to maintain ethical conduct and to cultivate specific qualities. They serve as the foundation for all further spiritual progress. • Concerning "the nature of the precepts": the precepts are rules of conduct designed to prevent harm to oneself and others. They are essential for creating the conditions necessary for inner peace and clarity. • On the subject of "the nature of the bodhisattva path": this is the path of the Mahāyāna follower who seeks to attain Buddhahood for the sake of all sentient beings. It is characterized by the six perfections and the four immeasurables. • Regarding "the nature of the tantric path": the tantric path utilizes skillful means to transform the ordinary body, speech, and mind into the pure forms of the deity. INTRODUCTION "I" The term "I" (*ahaṃ*) refers to the self (*ātman*). It is that which is designated as the "I" by means of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), which are the basis for the conceit of "I. It is not a permanent, unitary, or independent entity. This "I" is merely a conventional designation applied to the collection of conditioned phenomena; it does not exist as a substantial reality apart from these aggregates. Thus, when one says "I," one is referring to a conceptual construct superimposed upon the ever-changing flow of physical and mental processes. To realize this is to understand the teaching of non-self (*anātman*).

The meaning of the word "liberation" (mukti) is precisely that manifestation of the soul's own nature as Brahman— meaning the manifestation of supreme bliss and so forth— and it is also that absolute dissociation from the material qualities (guṇas), which constitutes non-identity with them; the point is that these are not two different things.
2. Here, "knowledge" (jñāna) refers to the supreme direct realization (sākṣātkāra) of Brahman.

The qualities of nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*) are described in the *Bhagavadgītā* as follows:

"Contemplation on its being" (*tadbhāvabhāvanā*) is the reflection upon the Self as "I am Brahman.

This is the meaning of the passage: when the knowledge of the direct realization of Brahman has arisen, because ignorance— also known by the name *avidyā*— is dissolved, and the resulting cognitions of difference have set, one attains and becomes the supreme light, which is the very nature of Brahman, [and exists] "in one's own form."
"He becomes manifest" (*abhiniṣpadyate*) means that he becomes revealed in his essential nature (*svābhāvika*), which consists of consciousness, bliss, and so forth.

Furthermore, Devala states that the purpose [of yoga] is fourfold: union (sāyujya), residence in the same world (sālokya), absorption into primordial nature (prakṛtilaya), and liberation (mokṣa). Through the method of attaining sovereignty over these, [one reaches] Hiraṇyagarbha and Nārāyaṇa—
The state of union (*sāyujya*) consists of becoming one in speech with the deities, beginning with Śiva, Mahendra, Soma, Sūrya, Skanda, Jyeṣṭhā, Umā, Devī, and others.

Attainment of the same world (*sālokya*) is not explicitly taught [as a distinct goal] because it is a specific form of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*). Dissolution into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*) consists of becoming a presiding deity (*adhidaivatattva*) among the elements such as earth and so forth, and being permeated by their state of being; this refers to [identification with] Earth, Fire, Varuṇa, Vāyu, and Sarasvatī—that is, Earth, Fire, Water, Air, and [Ether].

In the *Kāśī* [Upaniṣad], there is the state of being the locus (*ādheyatva*), the state of being the presiding deity (*adhidaivatātva*), and the state of being manifested through that [deity] (*tadbhāvabhāvitva*), which arises from specific yogic practices.

Restraining his speech, he should devote himself solely to the private recitation of the Veda. For him, clothing made of materials from the forest is prescribed. Thenceforth, he should live subsisting on roots, fruits, leaves, and grasses; finally, he should subsist on whatever comes to hand. Thereafter, he should take refuge in water, air, and space.

Among these, each subsequent combination is distinguished by its fruit. Alternatively, some teach a sequential order for the forest-dweller alone: having completed his studies, taken a wife, and established the sacred fires, he undertakes the ritual acts beginning with the Soma sacrifices.

It is heard that having built a house, he may dwell outside the village together with his wife, his offspring, and the sacred fires; or he may live alone, subsisting by gleaning ears of grain or picking up single grains. "Facing the sun, one should touch water"—this is the rule for touching water in all cases.

One should avoid alkaline substances, salt, honey, and meat. 28. [Page 111] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, should train in the perfection of giving. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift, he does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive a recipient of the gift, nor does he perceive the gift itself. This, Subhūti, is the perfection of giving of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, become one who has mounted on the perfection of morality? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated the thought of awakening, undertakes the training in the precepts of morality; he refrains from taking life, refrains from taking what is not given, refrains from sexual misconduct, refrains from false speech, refrains from malicious speech, refrains from harsh speech, refrains from idle chatter, refrains from covetousness, refrains from ill will, and refrains from wrong view. He does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive a being, nor does he perceive a soul, nor does he perceive a person. He does not perceive the training in the precepts of morality, nor does he perceive one who trains in the precepts of morality. This, Subhūti, is the perfection of morality of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, become one who has mounted on the perfection of patience? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated the thought of awakening, becomes patient toward all beings; he is patient with those who revile him, those who strike him, and those who insult him. He does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive a being, nor does he perceive a soul, nor does he perceive a person. He does not perceive patience, nor does he perceive one who practices patience. This, Subhūti, is the perfection of patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, become one who has mounted on the perfection of vigor? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated the thought of awakening, exerts vigor for the sake of the welfare of all beings; he does not weary of the cycle of existence. He does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive a being, nor does he perceive a soul, nor does he perceive a person. He does not perceive vigor, nor does he perceive one who exerts vigor. This, Subhūti, is the perfection of vigor of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, become one who has mounted on the perfection of meditation? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated the thought of awakening, enters into the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, and the formless attainments, yet he does not realize the reality-limit midway. He does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive a being, nor does he perceive a soul, nor does he perceive a person. He does not perceive meditation, nor does he perceive one who practices meditation. This, Subhūti, is the perfection of meditation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, become one who has mounted on the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated the thought of awakening, investigates all dharmas as empty of intrinsic nature. He does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive a being, nor does he perceive a soul, nor does he perceive a person. He does not perceive wisdom, nor does he perceive one who practices wisdom. This, Subhūti, is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, become one who has mounted on the six perfections? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the six perfections, nor does he perceive one who courses in them, nor does he perceive the fruit of those perfections, this, Subhūti, is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, becomes one who has mounted on the six perfections. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, become one who has mounted on the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated the thought of awakening, cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, yet he does not realize the reality-limit midway. He does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive a being, nor does he perceive a soul, nor does he perceive a person. He does not perceive the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, nor does he perceive one who cultivates them. This, Subhūti, is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, becomes one who has mounted on the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, become one who has mounted on the ten powers of a Tathāgata? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated the thought of awakening, understands as they really are the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible; he understands the ripening of karma according to its cause; he understands the various inclinations of beings; he understands the world with its many and different elements; he understands the faculties of other beings and other persons; he recollects his manifold past lives; he perceives with the divine eye the passing away and rebirth of beings; and he realizes the destruction of the taints through the knowledge that 'birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being. "The procedure for renunciation" (*sannyāsavidhi*) refers to the duties pertaining to the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśrama*). It includes all the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), beginning with the conception (*garbhādhāna*). For this very reason, one who has remained steadfast in the stage of studenthood (*brahmacarya*)—without having violated it—...

*Brahmacarya*: the word "of some" (*ekeṣām*) is understood as referring to their view. The grammatical construction is: "they teach renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) for a *vidhura*—that is, a man whose wife has died.
"*Karmavirāme*" means when the capacity for the performance of ritual acts has ceased. "'Eṣa'" refers to this [renunciation].

The designation "that by which the sun shines" refers to the Self mentioned in the Śruti; the word "of the Brāhmaṇa" is to be understood as the ellipsis. By this, he shows that the Brāhmaṇa has the qualification for renunciation (saṃnyāsa). And that eternal Self "does not increase through action, nor does it grow by merit."

"By no [means] less," the remainder being "by evil. "Of that very one," i.e., of the Supreme Brahman; "the Self" is its own nature. "A knower of the path" (*padavit*): here, "path" (*pada*) refers to the Veda, in the sense that it is "that by which [it] is reached" (*padyate gamyate anena*). "He prepares" means he makes it possible. "Staves" are three bamboo rods. "Vessel" [is mentioned].

"Begging bowl" (bhikṣāpātra). "'Trivṛt' means the three [substances] mixed together, such as clarified butter and so forth. "'He should fast' means he should not eat again. "'Or water' is an alternative in the absence of clarified butter and the other substances. "'By quarters' means by foot; 'by half-verses' means by half-verse; 'in its entirety' means by the whole."

"Separated" means devoid of the *vyāhṛtis*. "The self by the self," and so forth. By the word "Brahman," the *Sāvitrī* is meant here. The meaning is that one indeed becomes "purified," that is, cleansed of sin.

Furthermore, by the mention of the "hermitage" (*āśrama*), it is stated that after entering the *Sāvitrī* [initiation], there is no returning again. The remainder of the sentence is: "This very mendicant (*bhikṣu*) is fit for infinity. Having "kindled" (*upasamādhāya*) [the fire], i.e., having set it ablaze; and having "brought" [the materials]—even in the case of those of different origins—at the sacred place (*āyatana*).
Having placed [the firewood], he kindles it. Having added a fuel-stick (*samidh*) made of *pālāśa* wood measuring a span (*prādeśa*),
and having removed [the ashes] from the Āhavanīya fire, having spread out grass-blades, *darbha* stalks, sacrificial vessels (*yajñāyudha*),
and a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) as an interlayer, and having strewn them upon the *darbha* grass, [he performs the rite] even at an improper time.
Having spread the *pṛṣṭhyā* line as before, one should lay down a row of *ulapa* grass between the *gārhapatya* and *āhavanīya* fires.

having made [vessels] that are not made of clay or stone— namely, those distinct from being made of clay or stone.

The word "vaditi" is for the purpose of prohibiting the wearing of the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*prācīnāvīti*). The hymn beginning with "Om is Brahman" and ending with "the Self is light" is the *oṃkāra*.
Immediately after the worship of the Sun, one should repeat the Sāvitrī mantra one thousand times.

"Purified" means not having had impure substances removed by means of inspection and other such methods. Now, regarding the duties of an ascetic (yati): immediately after the statement concerning the mendicant's desire for absorption into Brahman through Sāṃkhya and Yoga, Hārīta says:

Desiring that very liberation, having extinguished the fires abiding within himself, having renounced the staffs of mind, speech, and action, and having granted fearlessness to all beings, he should go to the forest and not return;
being without fire, without a fixed dwelling, providing for no more than the morrow, shaven-headed, and wearing ochre-colored garments...

Holding in his hand the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), the water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*), and the water-strainer (*pavitra*) for the purpose of warding off minute living beings, he has abandoned the nature of the "staff"— which refers to mental, verbal, and physical actions that cause harm to others— and for the sake of granting fearlessness to all beings, he has gone to the forest to cease [all such] activity.

One should always wander alone for the sake of accomplishment, without a companion;

remaining seated, delighting in the inner self, indifferent to worldly objects, and free from sensual desire.

Seeking happiness, one should wander here with oneself alone as a companion,
with hair, nails, and beard trimmed, carrying a staff, a bowl, and a water-strainer.
He should always wander about with self-restraint, never causing pain to any living beings,
for the sake of protecting all creatures, both by night and by day.
When his body is exhausted, he should travel across the earth after careful consideration;
generally, he should wander during the eight months of summer and winter.
For the sake of the welfare of all beings, one should dwell in one place during the rainy season.
By the word "alone," the abandonment of those previously known is expressed;
by the phrase "without a companion," he states the abandonment even of those not previously known. "Success for one..."

"Of one" means: seeing the perfection of that single person who is free from all attachments and empty of the sense of "mine," one should wander alone. Otherwise, having formed an attachment to sons and others, one neither abandons them nor is one liberated from them—this is the meaning. [As it is said: "Scattered across the seven gates..."

The six sense organs are "mind" (miti); intellect (buddhi) is the seventh. Since speech operates upon objects grasped by these, they are called the "gateways" (dvārāṇi) of speech. Therefore, one should not utter speech that refers to objects grasped by these [senses], but rather one should speak only that which has liberation as its basis; such is the meaning.

In the section on liberation (mokṣakāṇḍa), there is the duty of the ascetic (yatidharma) and likewise Yama.

Through the restraint of the senses, through the destruction of passion and hatred,
and through non-violence toward living beings, one becomes fit for immortality.
Free from possessiveness, free from egoism, free from expectations, and free from worldly desire—
he who wanders alone by himself shall be happy.

providing only for the day without storing for the morrow.
Dwelling in an empty house, in caves, on mountains, by rivers,
at the edge of a village, at the foot of a tree, or even in a clean temple.

Bhagavadgītā, Chapter 18, Verses 1–12. [Page 238] The Blessed Lord said: Now I shall declare to you, who do not cavil, the knowledge among all knowledges which, when known, bestows final liberation and the supreme good. Among the various types of knowledge, this is considered the highest: the realization that the Supreme Being is one, and that all beings exist within Him; and that He exists within all beings. Those who perceive with an eye of wisdom that the manifold existence of beings is rooted in One, and that from that same One it emanates—they attain the Supreme. This world is deluded by the pairs of opposites arising from desire and aversion. Therefore, O descendant of Bharata, those who are unenlightened do not strive for liberation. But those who are steadfast and whose wisdom is established in the Self, having subdued these pairs of opposites, O Arjuna, proceed toward liberation. That which is night for all beings is the time of waking for the disciplined sage; and that which is the day of all beings is the time of night for the seer. For him who has transcended both pleasure and pain, and whose wisdom is firmly grounded, there is nothing further to be attained beyond the realization of the Absolute. He who is equanimous amidst the cold and the heat, amidst pleasure and pain, and who is indifferent to honor and dishonor, is fit for the state of Brahman. He to whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal; to whom the pleasant and the unpleasant are the same; who is impartial toward praise and blame; who remains the same in honor and dishonor; who is the same toward friend and foe; and who has renounced all undertakings—he alone is called a sage who has attained perfection. One should lift oneself up by means of the self, and never allow oneself to sink down; for the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self. The self is the friend of the self for that person whose self has been conquered by the self through yoga; but for one whose self is unsubdued, the self acts as an adversary, like an enemy. [Page 239] The supreme Self dwells in the hearts of all beings, causing them—through the machine of Maya—to revolve by means of the wheel of illusion. With the sword of non-dual knowledge, sharpened by the whetstone of meditation, one should sever the bonds of birth consisting of the seeds of karma. One should seek refuge in that Intelligence which is beyond the intellect, by means of the mind that is absorbed in the Supreme. Having thereby subdued the entire range of the senses and the mind, one should remain steadfast in the Self alone. Having cast off all desires, and completely restraining the entire group of the senses on every side, one should gradually attain tranquility through the intellect focused on the Self, and should not think of anything else. When the mind, having been restrained, becomes steady in the Self and finds no other support, then it attains the supreme bliss born of contact with the Brahman. One should know that the agitation of the mind arises from the objects of the senses; therefore, one should restrain the senses on all sides from the objects of sense-perception. He whose senses are fully withdrawn from their objects is one whose intellect is firmly established. But for him whose senses are not controlled, his discernment is carried away. Having brought the restless and fickle mind under control by the practice of yoga, one should remain vigilant, fixing the heart upon Me alone, O son of Kuntī. For one who meditates upon Me, with the mind fixed on Me and having attained Me as the supreme goal, I am easily accessible, O Partha, because he is ever devoted to Me. ||| 18.63 || Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Liberation through Renunciation," in the Bhagavad Gītā, the Scripture of Divine Wisdom and the Sacred Dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, contained within the Bhīṣma Parva of the Mahābhārata. ||| 18.64 || [Page 238] 15] The Blessed Lord said: Now I shall declare to you, who do not cavil, the knowledge among all knowledges which, when known, bestows final liberation and the supreme good. In the section on liberation, regarding the yoga of knowledge and action:
He who has renounced does not hate unwholesome action nor does he cling to wholesome action;
he is permeated by purity, wise, and his doubts are severed.
Indeed, it is not possible for one who bears a body to abandon actions entirely;
however, he who renounces the fruits of action is called a "renouncer."
The threefold fruit of action— unpleasant, pleasant, and mixed—
accrues after death to those who do not renounce, but never to those who have renounced.

"Having abandoned attachment" means indeed having abandoned the fruits such as worship and other fruits intended for unseen purposes (adṛṣṭārtha). "Of the obligatory" refers to that which is constant and occasional (nitya-naimittika).
"He hates the unwholesome" refers to that which brings about suffering, such as contempt, verbal abuse, and physical assault.
"He does not hate" means that, realizing "I am experiencing the fruit of past karma," he remains tranquil. "In the wholesome" refers to that which brings about happiness, such as honor and worship.
In that very way,
he who performs the necessary action without depending on the fruit of action, [is a yogi].
He is both a renunciant and a yogi; he is not one who maintains no sacred fires, nor is he one who performs no actions.
That which they call renunciation, know that to be yoga, O Pāṇḍava;
for no one becomes a yogin without having renounced purposeful volition.
For the sage who seeks to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means.
But for that person who rejoices only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self,
and who finds contentment in the Self alone— for him there is no duty to be performed.
He has no purpose whatsoever here through action, nor any at all through inaction;
nor does he have any dependence on any being for any object of desire.

Therefore, always perform the action that must be done without attachment;
for by performing action without attachment, a person attains the Supreme.
For Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone;
you should also act, having regard for the maintenance of the world.
Whatever a superior person practices, that very thing other people do;
whatever standard he sets, the world follows that.
O Pārtha, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that must be done by me;
there is nothing unattained to be attained, yet I continue to engage in action.
For if I were not to engage in action tirelessly at any time,
O Pārtha, men would follow my path in every respect.
These worlds would perish if I were not to perform action;
I would be the author of confusion and would destroy these beings.
Just as the ignorant act while attached to action, O Bhārata,
so should the wise man act without attachment, desiring the welfare of the world.

A wise man, acting with disciplined composure, should not create a disturbance in the minds of the ignorant who are attached to action; rather, he should encourage them toward all actions while performing them himself.

He whose delight is in the Self alone and not in sense objects is "one who delights in the Self" (ātmarati). He who is satisfied in the Self alone and not by food, flavors, and so forth, is "satisfied in the Self" (ātmatṛpta). He who is contented in the Self alone is "contented in the Self" (ātmasantuṣṭa); for him, there is no further task to be accomplished through the acquisition of wealth.

For one who has attained the supreme light, there is no longer any worldly activity; therefore, he has no duty to perform. Due to the absence of any cause for qualification (*adhikāra*), there is no purpose—characterized by the non-arising of demerit (*pratyavāya*) caused by performing prohibited acts—to be achieved through the non-performance of what is forbidden. [The word] "purpose" (*artha*)...

"Reliance" is the expectation of a motive; since the renunciation of action does not arise for one who follows worldly conventions, therefore, being free from desire for the fruits of action, that which must necessarily be done [should be performed].

272. If one were to ask, "How many types of persons (pudgala) are there? the answer is: there are seven types of persons. Which seven? They are: the person who is a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), the person who is a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), the person who is a non-returner (anāgāmin), the person who is an arhat, the person who is a pratyekabuddha, the person who is a bodhisattva, and the person who is a tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly enlightened one (samyaksaṃbuddha). These are the seven types of persons. What is the definition of a person who is a stream-enterer? One who has attained the fruit of stream-entry is called a person who is a stream-enterer. What is the definition of a person who is a once-returner? One who has attained the fruit of once-returning is called a person who is a once-returner. What is the definition of a person who is a non-returner? One who has attained the fruit of non-returning is called a person who is a non-returner. What is the definition of a person who is an arhat? One who has attained the fruit of arhatship is called a person who is an arhat. What is the definition of a person who is a pratyekabuddha? One who has attained the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha is called a person who is a pratyekabuddha. What is the definition of a person who is a bodhisattva? One who has generated the mind for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and is training on the path is called a person who is a bodhisattva. What is the definition of a person who is a tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly enlightened one? One who has realized unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is called a person who is a tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly enlightened one. These are the seven types of persons. What is the definition of a person who is a stream-enterer? It is the state of having entered the stream; therefore, one is called a person who is a stream-enterer. What is the definition of a person who is a once-returner? Because they will return to this world only once more, they are called a person who is a once-returner. What is the definition of a person who is a non-returner? Because they will not return to this world again, they are called a person who is a non-returner. What is the definition of a person who is an arhat? Because they have destroyed all defilements, they are called a person who is an arhat. What is the definition of a person who is a pratyekabuddha? Because they awaken by themselves without a teacher, they are called a person who is a pratyekabuddha. What is the definition of a person who is a bodhisattva? Because they seek to save all sentient beings, they are called a person who is a bodhisattva. What is the definition of a person who is a tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly enlightened one? Because they have come from suchness (tathatā), they are called a tathāgata; because they have destroyed all defilements, they are called an arhat; and because they have awakened to all phenomena, they are called a perfectly enlightened one. These are the seven types of persons. What is the definition of a person who is a stream-enterer? It is the state of having entered the stream of the noble ones; therefore, one is called a person who is a stream-enterer. What is the definition of a person who is a once-returner? Because they will return to this world only once more, they are called a person who is a once-returner. What is the definition of a person who is a non-returner? Because they will not return to this world again, they are called a person who is a non-returner. What is the definition of a person who is an arhat? Because they have destroyed the enemy of the defilements, they are called a person who is an arhat. What is the definition of a person who is a pratyekabuddha? Because they awaken to the Dharma by themselves, they are called a person who is a pratyekabuddha. What is the definition of a person who is a bodhisattva? Because they possess great compassion and seek to benefit others, they are called a person who is a bodhisattva. What is the definition of a person who is a tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly enlightened one? Because they have come from suchness, they are called a tathāgata; because they have destroyed all defilements, they are called an arhat; and because they have awakened to all phenomena, they are called a perfectly enlightened one. These are the seven types of persons. What is the definition of a person who is a stream-enterer? It is the state of having entered the stream of the noble ones; therefore, one is called a person who is a stream-enterer. What is the definition of a person who is a once-returner? 281. "The Blessed One said this: 'Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking birth. 281. "Monks, what are these four? They are: edible food, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. 281. "Monks, these are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking birth. 281. "Monks, I say that the cessation of craving is the abandonment of these four nutriments, their relinquishment, their emancipation, and their non-arising in the future. 281. "Monks, when a noble disciple understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these four nutriments, then, monks, this noble disciple is called one who has cut off craving, removed the fetters, and through the complete destruction of pride, has attained final Nibbāna in this very life. 281. "Monks, it is in this way that the Dhamma is well-expounded by me, clear, open, evident, leading onward, accessible, and to be realized by the wise, each for themselves. 281. 285. “‘[The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who goes from darkness to darkness; the person who goes from darkness to light; the person who goes from light to darkness; and the person who goes from light to light. And how, monks, is one a person who goes from darkness to darkness? Here, monks, someone is reborn in a low family—a family of outcasts, bamboo-workers, hunters, chariot-makers, or flower-scavengers—one that is poor, with little food and drink, where sustenance is obtained with difficulty, and which is full of suffering, crowded with hunger and thirst. And he is himself ugly, unsightly, ill-favored, with a deformed body, blind, crippled, lame, or paralyzed. He does not possess wealth, grain, silver, gold, property, or possessions. And he performs evil deeds by way of body, speech, and mind. Having performed and accumulated such actions, at the breaking up of the body after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, an evil destination, a lower realm, or in hell. This, monks, is called a person who goes from darkness to darkness. And how, monks, is one a person who goes from darkness to light? Here, monks, someone is reborn in a low family—as previously described—and he is himself ugly, unsightly, ill-favored, with a deformed body, blind, crippled, lame, or paralyzed. He does not possess wealth, grain, silver, gold, property, or possessions. But he performs wholesome deeds by way of body, speech, and mind. Having performed and accumulated such actions, at the breaking up of the body after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world. This, monks, is called a person who goes from darkness to light. And how, monks, is one a person who goes from light to darkness? Here, monks, someone is reborn in a high family—one of the Khattiyas, Brahmins, or householders—abundant in wealth, with great possessions, great enjoyments, and vast property. And he is himself handsome, attractive, graceful, possessing supreme beauty of form, neither blind nor crippled, nor lame, nor paralyzed. He possesses wealth, grain, silver, gold, property, and possessions. But he performs evil deeds by way of body, speech, and mind. Having performed and accumulated such actions, at the breaking up of the body after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, an evil destination, a lower realm, or in hell. This, monks, is called a person who goes from light to darkness. And how, monks, is one a person who goes from light to light? 42. [Page 411] The Blessed One said this: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as gross nutriment, contact as the second, mental volition as the third, and consciousness as the fourth. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said: "Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard it, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. "Ānanda, if anyone should say: 'Without depending on the nutriment of physical food as gross nutriment, I shall maintain myself,' that would be impossible. For what reason? Because, Ānanda, this is the nature of things: that beings who have come to be subsist by means of nutriment. [The Buddha then proceeds to explain each of the four nutriments in detail, including their origin, cessation, and the path leading to their cessation. "Ānanda, when a noble disciple has abandoned ignorance and aroused true knowledge, he abandons the nutriment of physical food, he abandons the nutriment of contact, he abandons the nutriment of mental volition, and he abandons the nutriment of consciousness. Having abandoned them, he does not cling to anything in the world; not clinging, he is not agitated; being unagitated, he personally attains Nibbāna. He understands: 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, the Venerable Ānanda rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks!"—"Venerable sir," they replied. The Blessed One said this: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as gross nutriment, contact as the second, mental volition as the third, and consciousness as the fourth. And what, monks, is the nutriment of physical food as gross nutriment? It is the edible food, whether coarse or subtle, whether material or non-material, whether derived from the earth or from space, whether past, future, or present—this is called the nutriment of physical food as gross nutriment. And what, monks, is the nutriment of contact? Whatever contact there is, whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, through the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind—this is called the nutriment of contact. And what, monks, is the nutriment of mental volition? Whatever volition there is, whether directed toward the realm of sense-desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm—this is called the nutriment of mental volition. And what, monks, is the nutriment of consciousness? Whatever consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—this is called the nutriment of consciousness. Now, monks, the nutriment of physical food as gross nutriment has its source in craving; craving has its source in feeling; feeling has its source in contact; contact has its source in the six sense bases; the six sense bases have their source in name-and-form; name-and-form has its source in consciousness; consciousness has its source in kamma-formations; and kamma-formations have their source in ignorance. But when ignorance is abandoned and true knowledge arises, monks, kamma-formations cease; with the cessation of kamma-formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, grasping ceases; with the cessation of grasping, becoming ceases; with the cessation of becoming, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will abandon ignorance and arouse true knowledge. Thus, monks, should you train yourselves. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those monks rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
